independent_variables.name: Holder67
independent_variables.definition: CEO option-based overconfidence indicator: C̄ is the value of exercisable unexercised options divided by the number of exercisable unexercised options; X̄ is the fiscal-year-end stock price S̄ minus C̄. Holder67 equals one when C̄/X̄ exceeds 0.67 at least twice during the sample period, zero otherwise. A CEO is classified as overconfident beginning in the first qualifying fiscal year and remains so through the rest of the sample. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

+ β 27 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> OverCont −1 + βFirm + βYear + ε, (1)
Holder67 is equal to one when the ratio of the value of options in-the-money to the average strike price exceeds 0.67 at least twice during the sample period, zero otherwise.

Consistent with Malmendier and Tate [2005] and Campbell et al. [2011], a CEO is classified as overconfident in the first fiscal year he/she exhibits the overconfident behavior and continues to be classified as overconfident for the remainder of the sample.

we set Holder67 (overconfidence) equal to one when the ratio of the options in-the-money ( C <sup> ̄</sup> / X <sup> ̄</sup> ) exceeds 0.67 at least twice during the sample
period, zero otherwise. Consistent with Malmendier and Tate [2005] and
Campbell et al. [2011], a CEO is classified as overconfident in the first fiscal year he/she exhibits the overconfident behavior and continues to be
classified as overconfident for the remainder of the sample.

independent_variables.name: D × Purchase
independent_variables.definition: CEO purchase-based overconfidence indicator: net purchases are purchases minus sales; the measure equals one when net purchases are in the top quintile of all CEO net purchases and the purchases increase the CEO’s ownership in the firm by 10% during the fiscal year, zero otherwise. Purchases due to option exercises are excluded. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

evidence.quote:
NI t = β 0 + β 1 Dt + β 2 Ownt −1 + β 3 MTBt −1 + β 4 Leverage t −1

+ β 5 Firm Sizet −1 + β 6 Litigationt −1 + β 7 OverCont −1

+ β 8D t <sup>∗</sup> Ownt −1 + β 9 Dt <sup>∗</sup> MTBt −1 + β 10 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Leverage t −1
+ β 11D t <sup>∗</sup> Firm Sizet −1 + β 12 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Litigationt −1 + β 13 Dt <sup>∗</sup> OverCont −1

+ β 14 Returnt + β 15 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Ownt −1 + β 16 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> MTBt −1

+ β 17 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Leverage t −1 + β 18 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Firm Sizet −1

+ β 19 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Litigationt −1 + β 20 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> OverCont −1

+ β 21 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt + β 22 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Ownt −1

+ β 23 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> MTBt −1 + β 24 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Leverage t −1
+ β 25 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Firm Sizet −1 + β 26 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Litigationt −1
+ β 27 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> OverCont −1 + βFirm + βYear + ε, (1)
D is an indicator variable set equal to one if Return is negative, zero otherwise
Return is the annual buy and hold return beginning four months after the prior fiscal year end

Purchase is equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases (purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm by 10%, zero otherwise.

Thus, consistent with
Campbell et al. [2011], we classify a CEO as overconfident using a dichotomous variable where Purchase is set equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases
(purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm
by 10% during the fiscal year, otherwise zero.

In our Purchase measure, we exclude purchases due to option exercises, although our
results remain qualitatively similar to those reported if we include purchases due to option
transactions.

independent_variables.name: Return × Purchase
independent_variables.definition: CEO purchase-based overconfidence indicator: net purchases are purchases minus sales; the measure equals one when net purchases are in the top quintile of all CEO net purchases and the purchases increase the CEO’s ownership in the firm by 10% during the fiscal year, zero otherwise. Purchases due to option exercises are excluded. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

evidence.quote:
NI t = β 0 + β 1 Dt + β 2 Ownt −1 + β 3 MTBt −1 + β 4 Leverage t −1

+ β 5 Firm Sizet −1 + β 6 Litigationt −1 + β 7 OverCont −1

+ β 8D t <sup>∗</sup> Ownt −1 + β 9 Dt <sup>∗</sup> MTBt −1 + β 10 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Leverage t −1
+ β 11D t <sup>∗</sup> Firm Sizet −1 + β 12 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Litigationt −1 + β 13 Dt <sup>∗</sup> OverCont −1

+ β 14 Returnt + β 15 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Ownt −1 + β 16 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> MTBt −1

+ β 17 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Leverage t −1 + β 18 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Firm Sizet −1

+ β 19 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Litigationt −1 + β 20 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> OverCont −1

+ β 21 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt + β 22 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Ownt −1

+ β 23 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> MTBt −1 + β 24 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Leverage t −1
+ β 25 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Firm Sizet −1 + β 26 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Litigationt −1
+ β 27 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> OverCont −1 + βFirm + βYear + ε, (1)
Return is the annual buy and hold return beginning four months after the prior fiscal year end

Purchase is equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases (purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm by 10%, zero otherwise.

Thus, consistent with
Campbell et al. [2011], we classify a CEO as overconfident using a dichotomous variable where Purchase is set equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases
(purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm
by 10% during the fiscal year, otherwise zero.

In our Purchase measure, we exclude purchases due to option exercises, although our
results remain qualitatively similar to those reported if we include purchases due to option
transactions.

independent_variables.definition: CEO purchase-based overconfidence indicator: net purchases are purchases minus sales; the measure equals one when net purchases are in the top quintile of all CEO net purchases and the purchases increase the CEO’s ownership in the firm by 10% during the fiscal year, zero otherwise. Purchases due to option exercises are excluded. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

D is an indicator variable set equal to one if Return is negative, zero otherwise

Return is the annual buy and hold return beginning four months after the prior fiscal year end

Purchase is equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases (purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm by 10%, zero otherwise.

Thus, consistent with
Campbell et al. [2011], we classify a CEO as overconfident using a dichotomous variable where Purchase is set equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases
(purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm
by 10% during the fiscal year, otherwise zero.

In our Purchase measure, we exclude purchases due to option exercises, although our
results remain qualitatively similar to those reported if we include purchases due to option
transactions.

independent_variables.name: Holder67
independent_variables.definition: CEO option-based overconfidence indicator: C̄ is the value of exercisable unexercised options divided by the number of exercisable unexercised options; X̄ is the fiscal-year-end stock price S̄ minus C̄. Holder67 equals one when C̄/X̄ exceeds 0.67 at least twice during the sample period, zero otherwise. A CEO is classified as overconfident beginning in the first qualifying fiscal year and remains so through the rest of the sample. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

evidence.quote:
Cont = β 0 + β 1 OverCont −1 + β 2 Ownt + β 3 MTBt + β 4 Leverage t

+ β 5 Firm Sizet + β 6 Litigationt + β 7 Sales Growtht + β 8 R & D ADt

+ β 9 CFO 1 + β 10 σ Revenuet + βFirm + βYear + ε, (6)
Holder67 is equal to one when the ratio of the value of options in-the-money to the average strike price exceeds 0.67 at least twice during the sample period, zero otherwise.

Consistent with Malmendier and Tate [2005] and Campbell et al. [2011], a CEO is classified as overconfident in the first fiscal year he/she exhibits the overconfident behavior and continues to be classified as overconfident for the remainder of the sample.

Second, we subtract ( C <sup> ̄</sup> ) from the stock price ( S <sup> ̄</sup> ) at the

we divide the average value per option ( C <sup> ̄</sup> ) by the average exercise price

independent_variables.name: Purchase
independent_variables.definition: CEO purchase-based overconfidence indicator: net purchases are purchases minus sales; the measure equals one when net purchases are in the top quintile of all CEO net purchases and the purchases increase the CEO’s ownership in the firm by 10% during the fiscal year, zero otherwise. Purchases due to option exercises are excluded. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

evidence.quote:
Cont = β 0 + β 1 OverCont −1 + β 2 Ownt + β 3 MTBt + β 4 Leverage t

+ β 5 Firm Sizet + β 6 Litigationt + β 7 Sales Growtht + β 8 R & D ADt

+ β 9 CFO 1 + β 10 σ Revenuet + βFirm + βYear + ε, (6)

Purchase is equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases (purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm by 10%, zero otherwise.

Thus, consistent with
Campbell et al. [2011], we classify a CEO as overconfident using a dichotomous variable where Purchase is set equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases
(purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm
by 10% during the fiscal year, otherwise zero.

In our Purchase measure, we exclude purchases due to option exercises, although our
results remain qualitatively similar to those reported if we include purchases due to option
transactions.

independent_variables.name: Purchase
independent_variables.definition: CEO purchase-based overconfidence indicator: net purchases are purchases minus sales; the measure equals one when net purchases are in the top quintile of all CEO net purchases and the purchases increase the CEO’s ownership in the firm by 10% during the fiscal year, zero otherwise. Purchases due to option exercises are excluded. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

evidence.quote:
Cont = β 0 + β 1 OverCont −1 + β 2 Ownt + β 3 MTBt + β 4 Leverage t

+ β 5 Firm Sizet + β 6 Litigationt + β 7 Sales Growtht + β 8 R & D ADt

+ β 9 CFO 1 + β 10 σ Revenuet + βFirm + βYear + ε, (6)

Purchase is equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases (purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm by 10%, zero otherwise.

Thus, consistent with
Campbell et al. [2011], we classify a CEO as overconfident using a dichotomous variable where Purchase is set equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases
(purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm
by 10% during the fiscal year, otherwise zero.

In our Purchase measure, we exclude purchases due to option exercises, although our
results remain qualitatively similar to those reported if we include purchases due to option
transactions.

independent_variables.definition: CEO option-based overconfidence indicator: C̄ is the value of exercisable unexercised options divided by the number of exercisable unexercised options; X̄ is the fiscal-year-end stock price S̄ minus C̄. Holder67 equals one when C̄/X̄ exceeds 0.67 at least twice during the sample period, zero otherwise. A CEO is classified as overconfident beginning in the first qualifying fiscal year and remains so through the rest of the sample. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

Holder67 is equal to one when the ratio of the value of options in-the-money to the average strike price exceeds 0.67 at least twice during the sample period, zero otherwise.

Consistent with Malmendier and Tate [2005] and Campbell et al. [2011], a CEO is classified as overconfident in the first fiscal year he/she exhibits the overconfident behavior and continues to be classified as overconfident for the remainder of the sample.

independent_variables.name: Purchase
independent_variables.definition: CEO purchase-based overconfidence indicator: net purchases are purchases minus sales; the measure equals one when net purchases are in the top quintile of all CEO net purchases and the purchases increase the CEO’s ownership in the firm by 10% during the fiscal year, zero otherwise. Purchases due to option exercises are excluded. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

evidence.quote:
Cont = β 0 + β 1 OverCont −1 + β 2 Ownt + β 3 MTBt + β 4 Leverage t

+ β 5 Firm Sizet + β 6 Litigationt + β 7 Sales Growtht + β 8 R & D ADt

+ β 9 CFO 1 + β 10 σ Revenuet + βFirm + βYear + ε, (6)

Purchase is equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases (purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm by 10%, zero otherwise.

Thus, consistent with
Campbell et al. [2011], we classify a CEO as overconfident using a dichotomous variable where Purchase is set equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases
(purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm
by 10% during the fiscal year, otherwise zero.

In our Purchase measure, we exclude purchases due to option exercises, although our
results remain qualitatively similar to those reported if we include purchases due to option
transactions.

review_notes: Source-first scope: the principal question is the relation between managerial overconfidence and accounting conservatism. Retain the full main regression family across the four stated conservatism outcomes and four overconfidence proxies: Table 4/equation (1), plus Tables 5–7/equation (6).

Tables 1–3 are descriptive/correlation analyses. Exclude the Table 8 external-monitoring interaction, CEO-turnover change tests, and other robustness or alternative-estimation exercises as separate follow-up questions.

Equation (5) uses Return_t and RET_t in different interaction blocks. Equation (2) and the page 9 definition identify these as the same annual return measure; the extraction preserves the printed notation and does not treat this as a substantive source conflict.

Underlying estimators are not named for the primary regressions or supporting fits. The Over-Invest construction fit also lacks its exact total-asset-growth formula, industry classification, fit sample, and per-fit N; the C-Score annual construction fit lacks the exact yearly sample and per-fit N.
results_review_notes: Tables 1 and 2 provide relevant raw descriptives for the retained baseline outcomes, proxies, controls, and asymmetric-timeliness variables. Table 3 is a correlation table and is not treated as descriptive statistics. Table 2 reports no exact p-values for its italicized 1% mean/median differences.
The CAPEX high-overconfidence Leverage median is visibly printed as 0.187 in Table 2; it is preserved verbatim rather than silently corrected.
